reads: the seventy odd cases in which I have during the last eight years studied the methods
text: Watson's notes span about eight years, so he is writing about eight years or more into knowing Holmes.

reads: the well-known Surrey family of the Roylotts of Stoke Moran
text: The case belongs to a known Surrey family, the Roylotts, at a place called Stoke Moran.

reads: a promise of secrecy was made at the time, from which I have only been freed during the last month by the untimely death of the lady to whom the pledge was given
text: A lady bound Watson to secrecy at the time of the events. She died only within the last month.

reads: there are widespread rumours as to the death of Dr. Grimesby Roylott
text: Dr. Grimesby Roylott is dead, and his death is the subject of public rumour.

reads: which tend to make the matter even more terrible than the truth
text: Watson concedes the truth is terrible but says the rumours are worse. Roylott's death is advertised in advance, so it is probably the point the story is heading for.
What is Roylott's part in this: the victim, or something darker?
options: Roylott is murdered and the case is to find who did it
Roylott is the wrongdoer and dies as a result of it
Roylott dies by some strange accident that gossip has made into a crime

text: A promise made 'at the time' of events is made to someone alive when those events are over or under way.
exceptions: A pledge could be given early in events the person did not outlive, though a pledge that lasts years implies the person lived on.

reads: It was early in April in the year ’83
text: The case opens in early April 1883.
If Watson writes up to about eight years into the partnership, around 1891, and the lady died only last month, she outlived these events by some years, perhaps as many as eight.

reads: a young lady has arrived in a considerable state of excitement, who insists upon seeing me
text: The client is a young lady, agitated, calling very early in the morning.
Perhaps this young lady is the lady of the pledge. She is the first woman to appear in a story that promised one.
A Victorian woman dressed wholly in black is often in mourning for a recent death.
exceptions: Black was also worn for sobriety, economy or inconspicuous travel.

reads: A lady dressed in black and heavily veiled
text: Black suggests she may have been bereaved. A heavy veil at this hour suggests she may not want to be recognised.
Veiled and desperate at dawn: she may have run away from something and come to London for good, hiding from a pursuer.
options: She has fled her home for good
She is only making a discreet visit

reads: It is fear, Mr. Holmes. It is terror.
text: Her shivering is from terror, by her own account, and her appearance bears it out.

reads: Her features and figure were those of a woman of thirty, but her hair was shot with premature grey
text: Grey hair at about thirty points to long strain. Whatever frightens her today may sit on top of something that has lasted years.
If she is the lady of the pledge, she comes through this danger alive and lives for years afterwards.
Someone who buys a return ticket means to travel back to where they started.
exceptions: Plans can change after purchase, and a return may be bought to mislead.

reads: I observe the second half of a return ticket in the palm of your left glove
text: She holds the unused return half of a railway ticket.
She has not fled for good. She bought a return and means to go back today.
Why would someone this terrified plan to go straight back?
options: She must be home before she is missed
She has nowhere else to go
What she fears is not at home

reads: The left arm of your jacket is spattered with mud in no less than seven places.
text: Fresh mud on her left sleeve is Holmes's evidence for a drive in a dog-cart.

reads: and then only when you sit on the left-hand side of the driver
text: If Holmes is right, she did not drive herself. Someone else took her, so at least one other person knows she set out this morning.

reads: I started from home before six, reached Leatherhead at twenty past
text: She left home before six, was at Leatherhead by 6.20, and took the first train to Waterloo.

reads: Whatever your reasons may be, you are perfectly correct
text: She confirms his conclusion, the early start and the drive, but she cannot vouch for his general rule about dog-carts. The conclusion stands on her word, not on the rule.
Leaving 'before six' and arriving at 6.20 means a drive of more than twenty minutes, probably not much over half an hour or so. Her home is within a few miles of Leatherhead.
Leatherhead is a town in Surrey, on a railway line into London.
Her home is in the Leatherhead district of Surrey, and the promised case concerns a Surrey family. That makes it more likely she is connected with the Roylotts and is the lady of the pledge.
She accounts for her times but says nothing of who drove her. A servant, a friend or a hired man? That person's loyalty could matter.

reads: I have no one to turn to—none, save only one, who cares for me, and he, poor fellow, can be of little aid
text: Only one man cares for her, and she says he cannot do much.
Why 'poor fellow'? Perhaps he is physically unable to help her, or far away or without means.
options: He is ill or infirm
He is absent
He is poor and powerless

reads: in a month or six weeks I shall be married, with the control of my own income
text: She will marry within about six weeks and will then control her own income.

reads: At present it is out of my power to reward you for your services
text: She has an income but does not control it now. Someone or something else holds it until she marries.
When an event would take money out of someone's hands, that person has a reason to wish the event prevented.
exceptions: Many people accept such a loss without resentment, and the sums may be too small to matter.

text: Her terror and her coming marriage may be linked. Whoever holds her income loses it when she marries, and the wedding gives a deadline of a month or six weeks.
options: The holder of her income is the danger
The marriage itself is the danger
Her fear has nothing to do with money
hindsight: She has not connected money with her fear. A first-time reader needs the genre habit of asking who loses when a woman comes into her own income.

text: If she belongs to the Roylott household, Dr. Roylott is the obvious candidate for whoever controls her money, or else he is a fellow target of the same danger.
options: Roylott controls her income and is what she fears
Roylott is threatened alongside her
Roylott is only incidental to her trouble
hindsight: She has not named Roylott or any relative. The link rests only on Watson's preamble and the Surrey location.

reads: it was concerned with an opal tiara
text: Mrs. Farintosh and the tiara explain how she found Holmes. Scenery for this case.

reads: my fears are so vague, and my suspicions depend so entirely upon small points
text: By her own account she has no open threat or solid proof, only small things that add up to fear.
'Small points, which might seem trivial' tells me to watch the trivial details in her account closely, because that is where the case will lie.

reads: even he to whom of all others I have a right to look for help and advice
text: The one man who cares, the man she has a right to look to, and her future husband are probably the same person: her fiance.

reads: looks upon all that I tell him about it as the fancies of a nervous woman
text: He is of little aid because he does not take her seriously, as far as she can tell. There is no need to suppose illness, absence or poverty.

reads: He does not say so, but I can read it from his soothing answers and averted eyes
text: His disbelief is her reading of his manner, not something he said. Averted eyes could mean embarrassment, pity or something he is hiding.
Should the fiance be trusted? He gains by the marriage and brushes off her fears, though nothing else counts against him.
options: He is sincere and merely sceptical
He has reason to keep her from looking closer

reads: you can see deeply into the manifold wickedness of the human heart
text: She believes a person is behind her danger, not chance or anything uncanny, and she appeals to Holmes on that basis.

reads: You may advise me how to walk amid the dangers which encompass me.
text: She asks how to live among dangers, not how to escape them. She expects to stay within reach of them, which fits the return ticket.
After all this she has given neither her own name nor that of anyone she fears, and she has not said what actually happened.
Open: who she is, what the 'small points' are, why she is in black, who drove her, who holds her income, why she is going back, and how Dr. Roylott comes into it.

Working picture: a woman of the Roylott circle in Surrey, perhaps recently bereaved, fears someone close to her as her wedding approaches, with money a possible reason. She probably survives, and Roylott's death comes out of this somehow.
options: The person she fears is the holder of her income
The person she fears is someone not yet mentioned
The danger is real but not aimed at her money
